lesson.title: When Formulas Have Several Letters
lesson.summary: Understand what a literal equation is, why formulas are written this way, and how to isolate one variable while treating the others as constants.
lesson.body:
Every equation solved so far has had exactly one variable, usually x, mixed with plain numbers. A literal equation is different: it contains two or more variables, such as A = lw or y = mx + b, and the goal is not to find a single number but to isolate one of the letters in terms of the others. Formulas in science, geometry, and finance are almost always written as literal equations, because a single formula like A = lw needs to work no matter what specific numbers l and w eventually take.

Solving a literal equation uses the exact same tools as solving equations with numbers: the addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division properties of equality. The only shift in thinking is treating every letter except the one you are solving for as if it were a fixed number, even though its value is not written out. Whatever operation is attached to the target variable gets undone with the inverse operation, applied to both sides, exactly as with a numeric equation.

Solve the perimeter formula P = 2l + 2w for w, treating P and l as known constants. Start by subtracting 2l from both sides: P - 2l = 2w. Then divide both sides by 2: (P - 2l)/2 = w, or equivalently w = (P - 2l)/2. To check this is correct, pick numbers: if l = 4 and w = 3, then P = 2(4) + 2(3) = 8 + 6 = 14. Substitute P = 14 and l = 4 into the new formula: w = (14 - 8)/2 = 6/2 = 3, which matches the original w = 3, confirming the rearrangement is correct.

A second example shows a case where the target variable is multiplied by two other letters rather than added to something. Solve the simple interest formula I = Prt for r, treating I, P, and t as known constants. Since r is multiplied by both P and t, divide both sides by the product Pt: I/(Pt) = r, or r = I/(Pt). Check with numbers: if P = 1000, t = 2, and r = 0.05, then I = 1000(0.05)(2) = 100. Substituting I = 100, P = 1000, and t = 2 into the rearranged formula gives r = 100/(1000 times 2) = 100/2000 = 0.05, which matches the original rate exactly.

This process depends on a solid understanding of what a variable represents: a placeholder for a number whose value can change, which is exactly why the same equation-solving property that undoes "+2l" for a numeric equation also undoes it here, even though 2l is not a single number but an expression built from two variables. The skill of isolating one letter in a literal equation is also the foundation for solving for a variable more generally and for manipulating formulas, both covered next in this unit.

Literal equations can look intimidating because there are more letters to track, but the underlying moves never change: identify what is attached to the target variable, then undo those operations in reverse order using the properties of equality, one letter or one number at a time, until that variable stands alone on one side.
